rules.title: Initial rent limit after voluntary vacancy
rules.requirement: For qualifying vacancy decontrol after a tenant voluntarily vacates, the landlord must limit the new tenant's initial rent increase to 25% over the prior tenant's last rent, excluding any capital improvement surcharge from that prior rent.
rules.key_value: 25% above prior rent, excluding capital improvement surcharge
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to a landlord setting a new tenant's initial rent under Article VII for a residential apartment in a dwelling registered in accordance with § 155-30, after the prior tenant voluntarily vacates without harassment, duress or unreasonable pressure from the landlord or the landlord's agents. The unit may not be decontrolled more than once in any three-year period. This finding addresses the expressly described voluntary-vacancy calculation; application of that calculation after eviction requires review.
rules.exemptions: Any capital improvement surcharge included in the prior tenant's last rent is excluded from the comparison amount.
rules.quoted_span: Provided that a dwelling is registered in accordance with § 155-30 upon the vacation of a residential apartment unit by a tenant, the apartment unit shall become decontrolled and exempt from the provisions of this chapter for the new tenant's initial rental; provided, however, that said rental shall be limited to an increase of 25% over the last rental paid by the tenant who voluntarily vacated the rental unit, exclusive of any capital improvement surcharge that is a component of said last rental.

rules.title: Subsequent increases and new base rent
rules.requirement: After the new tenant's initial rent under vacancy decontrol, additional rent increases must comply with Chapter 155. Computations under that chapter must use the initial base rent charged to the new tenant under § 155-31 as the base rent.
rules.key_value: Initial rent becomes the base rent
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to landlords imposing additional increases, and computations under Chapter 155, after a new tenant receives an initial rent under Article VII vacancy decontrol of a residential apartment in a dwelling registered under § 155-30. Qualifying vacancy circumstances are voluntary departure without landlord or agent harassment, duress or unreasonable pressure, legal eviction, or departure resulting from a competent court's order; the court-order ground is unavailable for dispossession based on holding over after expiration of the tenant's term. Decontrol is limited to once in any three-year period. Disputed vacancy circumstances are determined by the Rent Control Board after a hearing.
rules.exemptions: The Article VII exemption is limited to the new tenant's initial rent.
rules.quoted_span: However, any additional rental increase beyond the initial rental of the new tenant shall be subject to the provisions of this chapter. For the purpose of any computations under this chapter, the initial base rent charged to the new tenant under this section shall be considered the base rent.

rules.title: Permitted vacancy circumstances and improper decontrol remedies
rules.requirement: A landlord may claim Article VII decontrol only for voluntary vacancy without landlord or agent harassment, duress or unreasonable pressure, legal eviction, or vacancy resulting from a competent court's order; the court-order ground excludes dispossession based on holding over after the tenant's term expires. The Rent Control Board decides disputed vacancy circumstances after a hearing and, if it finds a landlord seeking or having obtained decontrol after a vacancy outside the permitted circumstances, may rescind decontrol, with rent reverting to its pre-vacancy amount, and prosecute the landlord under § 155-21.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to landlords seeking or having obtained Article VII vacancy decontrol of residential apartment units. Article VII requires dwelling registration under § 155-30 and permits decontrol no more than once in any three-year period. Permitted vacancy grounds are voluntary departure without harassment, duress or unreasonable pressure from the landlord or the landlord's agents, legal eviction, or departure resulting from an order of a court of competent jurisdiction; the court-order ground is unavailable to a landlord receiving a dispossession order based on the tenant holding over after expiration of the term. The stated remedies require a Board finding that the tenant vacated under circumstances outside § 155-32.
rules.exemptions: The court-order ground does not include dispossession based on holding over after expiration of the tenant's term.
rules.quoted_span:
The landlord shall be entitled to decontrol the apartment unit under this article only under the following circumstances:

A.

If the tenant vacates the apartment voluntarily without harassment, duress or unreasonable pressure from the landlord or his agents or if the tenant is legally evicted.

B.
If the tenant vacates the apartment as a result of a court order from a court of competent jurisdiction. This ground shall not be available to a landlord who receives a court order to dispossess a tenant based upon the tenant holding over and continuing in possession of the premises after the expiration of his term. Whenever there is an issue as to the circumstances under which a tenant has vacated an apartment unit, that issue shall be determined by the Rent Control Board after a hearing.
If the Board finds that a landlord is seeking to decontrol or has decontrolled an apartment unit and the tenant has vacated the unit under circumstances other than those set forth in this section, the Rent Board may rescind the decontrol of the apartment unit, and the rent shall revert to that rental on the apartment unit prior to the vacation of the apartment, and prosecute the landlord for violation of the chapter under § 155-21 .

rules.title: Vacancy decontrol certificate and filing fee
rules.requirement: When an apartment is decontrolled under Article VII, the landlord must file the Rent Leveling Board's certificate with a $50 filing fee. The certificate must identify the vacating tenant, existing rent, circumstances of vacancy, new tenant, new rent and effective date of the new rent.
rules.key_value: $50 certificate filing fee
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to the landlord whenever an apartment unit is decontrolled under Article VII. Authorized decontrol concerns a residential apartment in a dwelling registered under § 155-30, following voluntary vacancy without landlord or agent harassment, duress or unreasonable pressure, legal eviction, or vacancy resulting from a competent court's order; the court-order ground excludes dispossession based on holding over after expiration of the tenant's term. Decontrol is limited to once in any three-year period, and disputed vacancy circumstances are decided by the Rent Control Board after a hearing. The filing trigger is decontrol under Article VII, not a tenant's application for housing.
rules.quoted_span: When any apartment unit is decontrolled under this article, the landlord shall file a certificate, provided by the Rent Leveling Board, including a filing fee in the amount of $50, indicating the name of the vacating tenant, the existing rental, the circumstances under which the tenant vacated the apartment unit, the name of the new tenant, the new rental and the effective date of the new rental.

rules.title: Decontrol limited to once in three years
rules.requirement: A landlord may not decontrol a dwelling unit under Article VII more than once in any three-year period.
rules.key_value: Once in any three-year period
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to landlords seeking Article VII vacancy decontrol of dwelling units. Article VII concerns residential apartments in dwellings registered under § 155-30 and requires voluntary vacancy without landlord or agent harassment, duress or unreasonable pressure, legal eviction, or vacancy resulting from a competent court's order; the court-order ground is unavailable for dispossession based on holding over after expiration of the tenant's term. Disputed vacancy circumstances are decided by the Rent Control Board after a hearing. The frequency restriction concerns decontrol under this article.
rules.quoted_span: No dwelling unit shall be decontrolled pursuant to this article more than once in any three-year period.

rules.title: Residential rental application fee limit
rules.requirement: A covered landlord or landlord's agent must not require an application or similar fee exceeding $50 to apply to lease or sublease residential rental property for dwelling purposes. Violators face penalties of up to $500 for a first offense, $750 for a second offense, and $1,000 for each subsequent offense, enforced through summary proceedings in the property's county Superior Court, Law Division, Special Civil Part upon a complaint by the Division of Consumer Affairs Director or Attorney General; following proceedings, the amount wrongfully charged must be remitted to the applicant or prospective tenant from the collected penalty.
rules.key_value: $50 as of 2026-10-01; subject to statutory annual adjustment
rules.exemptions: Dwelling units located in one-family or two-family dwellings offered for rent are exempt. New Jersey Real Estate Commission licensees are exempt unless they are the landlord of the residential rental property.

rules.title: Protection against retaliatory rent increases
rules.requirement: Any person or agent who threatens or takes a retaliatory rent increase against a residential tenant for protected activity is liable for the greater of actual damages or an award of one to three months' rent, plus suit costs and a reasonable attorney's fee. A qualifying rent-increase notice within six months creates a rebuttable presumption of retaliation, rebuttable only by clear and convincing evidence of no reprisal, sufficient independent justification, and the same action at the same time regardless of protected activity or belief in it; any lease or rental-agreement waiver is void and unenforceable.
rules.key_value: Retaliatory increases prohibited; six-month rebuttable presumption
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to any person or agent thereof threatening or taking reprisals against a tenant of residential premises because the tenant: commenced, proceeded with, or obtained relief in a judicial or administrative action seeking damages under or enforcement of federal, state, or local law, regulation, by-law, or ordinance regulating residential premises; exercised rights under chapter 164, section 124D; reported a violation or suspected violation of a health or building code or other law, regulation, or municipal by-law or ordinance regulating residential premises to the board of health, Boston commissioner of housing inspection, or another board regulating residential premises; reported or complained of such a violation or suspected violation in writing to the landlord or landlord's agent; organized or joined a tenants' union or similar organization; or made or expressed an intention to make a rent payment to an organization of unit owners under chapter 183A, section 6(c). For the rent-increase presumption, the tenant must receive notice of an increase within six months after the tenant commenced, proceeded with, or obtained relief in such an action, exercised such rights, made such a report or complaint, or organized or joined such a tenants' union, or within six months after another person took such action or actions on the tenant's behalf or in, or relating to, the building where the tenant resides. The six-month period governs the presumption and does not establish a time limit on the underlying reprisal liability. The presumption requires clear and convincing rebuttal evidence of no reprisal, sufficient independent justification, and that the action would have occurred in the same manner and at the same time regardless of tenants' protected activity or the belief that tenants engaged in it. Waivers in any lease or other rental agreement are void and unenforceable.
rules.quoted_span:
Section 18. Any person or agent thereof who threatens to or takes reprisals against any tenant of residential premises for the tenant's act of, commencing, proceeding with, or obtaining relief in any judicial or administrative action the purpose of which action is to obtain damages under, or otherwise enforce, any federal, state or local law, regulation, by-law or ordinance, which has as its objective the regulation of residential premises; or exercising the tenant's rights pursuant to section one hundred and twenty-four D of chapter one hundred and sixty-four; or reporting to the board of health or, in the city of Boston to the commissioner of housing inspection or to any other board having as its objective the regulation of residential premises a violation or a suspected violation of any health or building code or of any other municipal by-law or ordinance, or state or federal law or regulation which has as its objective the regulation of residential premises; or reporting or complaining of such violation or suspected violation in writing to the landlord or to the agent of the landlord; or for organizing or joining a tenants' union or similar organization, or for making or expressing an intention to make, a payment of rent to an organization of unit owners pursuant to paragraph (c) of section six of chapter one hundred and eighty-three A shall be liable for damages which shall not be less than one month's rent or more than three month's rent, or the actual damages sustained by the tenant, whichever is greater, and the costs of the suit, including a reasonable attorney's fee.
The receipt of any notice of termination of tenancy, except for nonpayment of rent, or, of increase in rent, or, of any substantial alteration in the terms of tenancy within six months after the tenant has commenced, proceeded with, or obtained relief in such action, exercised such rights, made such report or complaint, or organized or joined such tenants' union or within six months after any other person has taken such action or actions on behalf of the tenant or in, or relating to, the building in which the tenant resides, shall create a rebuttable presumption that such notice or other action is a reprisal against the tenant for engaging in such activities. Such presumption shall be rebutted only by clear and convincing evidence that such person's action was not a reprisal against the tenant and that such person had sufficient independent justification for taking such action, and would have in fact taken such action, in the same manner and at the same time the action was taken, regardless of tenants engaging in, or the belief that tenants had engaged in, activities protected under this section.
Any waiver of this provision in any lease or other rental agreement shall be void and unenforceable.

rules.title: Protection against retaliatory tenancy termination
rules.requirement: Any person or agent who threatens or takes retaliatory tenancy termination against a residential tenant for protected activity is liable for the greater of actual damages or an award of one to three months' rent, plus suit costs and a reasonable attorney's fee. A qualifying termination notice within six months, except for nonpayment of rent, creates a rebuttable presumption of retaliation, rebuttable only by clear and convincing evidence of no reprisal, sufficient independent justification, and the same action at the same time regardless of protected activity or belief in it; any lease or rental-agreement waiver is void and unenforceable.
rules.key_value: Retaliatory termination prohibited; six-month rebuttable presumption
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to any person or agent thereof threatening or taking reprisals against a tenant of residential premises because the tenant: commenced, proceeded with, or obtained relief in a judicial or administrative action seeking damages under or enforcement of federal, state, or local law, regulation, by-law, or ordinance regulating residential premises; exercised rights under chapter 164, section 124D; reported a violation or suspected violation of a health or building code or other law, regulation, or municipal by-law or ordinance regulating residential premises to the board of health, Boston commissioner of housing inspection, or another board regulating residential premises; reported or complained of such a violation or suspected violation in writing to the landlord or landlord's agent; organized or joined a tenants' union or similar organization; or made or expressed an intention to make a rent payment to an organization of unit owners under chapter 183A, section 6(c). For the termination presumption, the tenant must receive a notice of termination, except for nonpayment of rent, within six months after the tenant commenced, proceeded with, or obtained relief in such an action, exercised such rights, made such a report or complaint, or organized or joined such a tenants' union, or within six months after another person took such action or actions on the tenant's behalf or in, or relating to, the building where the tenant resides. Waivers in any lease or other rental agreement are void and unenforceable.
rules.exemptions: Termination notices for nonpayment of rent are excluded from the rebuttable presumption; the text does not make nonpayment a general exemption from reprisal liability.

rules.title: Notice of tenants’ rights when ending occupancy
rules.requirement: Covered landlords and foreclosing owners must provide the Notice of Tenants’ Rights and Resources when starting eviction, declining lease renewal, or asking a tenant or former homeowner to leave, delivering it together with the applicable termination notice. This is a notification requirement and does not establish permissible grounds for eviction.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to all landlords and foreclosing owners intending to end a tenancy or post-foreclosure occupancy of a unit in Boston, including purchasers of property out of foreclosure or from a bank or mortgage lender asking former owners or tenants to leave. Excludes residences in any hospital, skilled nursing facility or health facility, and residences in a nonprofit facility whose primary purpose is providing short-term treatment, assistance or therapy for alcohol, drug or other substance abuse.
rules.exemptions: Residences in any hospital, skilled nursing facility or health facility; residences in a nonprofit facility whose primary purpose is providing short-term treatment, assistance or therapy for alcohol, drug or other substance abuse.

rules.quoted_span:
The Housing Stability Notification Act (HSNA) is an Ordinance passed by the City of
Boston in October 2020 that requires any landlord planning to end a tenancy
agreement to provide the tenant with a Notice of Tenants’ Rights and Resources.
The HSNA requires that landlords give this Notice of Tenants’ Rights and Resources
to tenants when the landlord starts the eviction process, or when the landlord
decides to not offer the tenant a renewal of their lease agreement. The Notice of
Tenants’ Rights and Resources must be delivered at the same time as the Notice to
Quit.
The Notice of Tenants’ Rights and Resources must also be delivered to any tenant
that is asked to leave a property. For example, if someone is purchasing a property
out of foreclosure, or from a bank or a mortgage lender, they must provide this
Notice to the former owners of the property, or any tenants that live in the
property.

rules.title: Criminal-history inquiries, checks and disclosure
rules.requirement: Subject to the listed exemptions, rental housing providers must not ask about or use criminal history or criminal background checks in rental advertising, applications, tenant selection or decision-making, or require disclosure or authorization for release of criminal history.

Require disclosure or authorization for release of criminal history

rules.title: Proposed prohibition on lessors purchasing defined coordination services
rules.requirement: The bill would prohibit a real estate lessor, its agent or its subcontractor from subscribing to, contracting with or otherwise exchanging anything of value for a defined service provider’s services. For successful enforcement, the proposal would award plaintiffs court-determined action costs, reasonable attorney fees, expert fees and investigation costs, including awards to a successfully enforcing attorney general or municipality; on a plaintiff’s prompt motion, the court could award simple interest on actual damages from service of the pleading asserting the chapter claim through judgment, or a shorter period within that interval.
rules.exemptions: A residential dwelling unit is a house, apartment, accessory unit or other unit intended as a person’s primary residence, excluding inpatient medical care, licensed long-term care and detention or correctional facilities. A real estate lessor is an individual, corporation, partnership, association, joint-stock company, trust or unincorporated organization that owns real property and leases all or part of it as a residential dwelling unit. A service provider is a person performing a coordination function for any real estate lessor or rentor; person includes a natural person, corporation, partnership, limited liability company, firm or association. Coordination comprises collecting the specified historical or contemporaneous actual rent, price-change, supply, occupancy or lease-termination and renewal information, analyzing or processing that information, and recommending rental prices, lease terms, occupancy levels or another commercial term to a real estate lessor. Publication of a fair market rent calculated using publicly available data is excluded from a recommendation. Computation is included but is not required by the definition. These are qualifications of the regulated actors and services, not findings about actual activity at an address.
rules.citation: H.5222, 194th General Court, proposed G.L. c. 40Z, §§ 1, 2(a), 3(b), 3(d)
rules.quoted_span:
“Coordinate”, with respect to a service provider, the:
(i) collecting of historical or contemporaneous actual rent prices, price changes, supply levels, occupancy rates or lease or rental contract termination and renewal dates of residential dwelling units;
(ii) analyzing or processing of the information described in clause (i), including with the use of a system, software or process that uses computation; and
(iii) recommending of rental prices, lease terms, occupancy levels, or other commercial term to a real estate lessor, provided that publication of a fair market rent calculated using publicly available data shall not constitute a recommendation.
“Person”, any natural person, corporation, partnership, limited liability company, firm or association.
“Predispute arbitration agreement”, an agreement to arbitrate a dispute that has not yet arisen at the time of the making of the agreement.
“Predispute joint-action waiver”, an agreement, whether or not part of a predispute arbitration agreement, that would prohibit or waive the right of one of the parties to participate in a joint, class or collective action in a judicial, arbitral, administrative or other forum, concerning a dispute that has not yet arisen at the time of the making of the agreement.
“Real estate lessor”, any individual, corporation, partnership, association, joint-stock company, trust or unincorporated organization that owns real property and leases such property or any portion thereof in the form of a residential dwelling unit.
“Residential dwelling unit”, any house, apartment, accessory unit or other unit intended to be used as a person’s primary residence; provided, that “residential dwelling unit” shall not include inpatient medical care, licensed long-term care and detention or correctional facilities.
“Service provider”, any person that performs a coordination function for any real estate lessor or rentor.
Section 2. (a) No real estate lessor, or any agent or subcontractor thereof, shall subscribe to, contract with or otherwise exchange anything of value in return for the services of a service provider.
(b) No service provider shall facilitate an agreement to not compete among real estate lessors with respect to residential dwelling units.
Section 3. (a) A violation of this section shall also constitute an unfair method of competition, and a violation of the provisions of chapter 93 and chapter 93A. Nothing in this section shall impair or limit the applicability of either chapter or the antitrust laws, generally.
(b) Pursuant to a motion by the plaintiff promptly made, the court may award simple interest on actual damages sustained by the plaintiff for the period beginning on the date of service of the pleading of the plaintiff setting forth a claim under this chapter and ending on the date of judgment, or for any shorter period therein.
(c) At the election of the person alleging conduct constituting a violation of this section, or the named representative of a class or in a collective action alleging such conduct, no predispute arbitration agreement or predispute joint-action waiver shall be valid or enforceable with respect to a case which is filed under federal, tribal or state or local law and relates to a violation of this chapter.
(d) In the case of any successful action to enforce liability pursuant to this chapter, the costs of the action together with reasonable attorney fees, expert fees and the costs of investigation as determined by the court shall be awarded to plaintiffs. Costs and attorney fees, expert fees and the costs of investigation shall be awarded to the attorney general or municipality where the attorney general or municipality successfully enforces this chapter.

rules.title: Proposed prohibition on algorithmic rent setting and occupancy determinations
rules.requirement: The pending bill would prohibit lessors and landlords from employing, using or relying on a defined algorithmic device or coordinator to set or change rent or determine occupancy levels for residential dwelling units, subject to the definitions and product exclusions below. A violation would violate Chapter 93A, section 2 and carry a civil penalty of no more than $5,000 per violation, with each rent determination, increase or setting under subsection (b) counted separately; successful enforcement plaintiffs, including the attorney general or a municipality when successfully enforcing the chapter, would receive action costs, reasonable attorney fees, expert fees and investigation costs as determined by the court.
rules.key_value: Proposed prohibition; civil penalty up to $5,000 per violation
rules.exemptions: Address scope is a house, apartment, accessory unit or other unit intended for use as a primary residence in Massachusetts. An algorithmic device is a computational process derived from machine learning or other artificial intelligence techniques that processes or calculates nonpublic competitor data to advise a lessor or landlord about rent; it excludes trade-association reports published periodically but no more frequently than monthly that receive renter data and publish it in an aggregated and anonymous matter, and products used to establish rent or income limits under affordable-housing program guidelines of a local government, the commonwealth, the federal government or another political subdivision. These are product exclusions, not blanket exemptions for affordable-housing properties. A coordinator is any person operating an algorithmic device, software or data analytics service that performs a coordinating function for a residential rental property lessor or landlord, including a lessor or landlord performing that function for their own benefit. A coordinating function uses nonpublic competitor data and includes collecting specified rent, supply or termination and renewal data from two or more lessors or landlords; computationally analyzing or processing those data, including algorithm training; and recommending rental prices, lease renewal terms or ideal occupancy levels. Nonpublic competitor data must be information not widely available or easily accessible to the public, derived from or otherwise provided by another lessor or landlord, whether attributable to a particular competitor or anonymized. Person includes natural persons, corporations, partnerships, companies, trusts and associations of persons. The proposal does not prohibit all pricing tools, and this extraction does not establish that any actor or product meets these definitions.
rules.citation: Massachusetts S.2983, 194th General Court, proposed G.L. c. 186, § 15G(a)–(d)
rules.quoted_span:
Section 15G. (a) As used in this section, the following words shall have the following meanings unless the context clearly requires otherwise:
"Algorithmic device", any computational process derived from machine learning or other artificial intelligence techniques, that processes or calculates nonpublic competitor data for the purpose of advising a lessor or landlord concerning the amount of rent that the lessor or landlord may consider charging a tenant; provided, however that "algorithmic device" shall not include: (i) any report published periodically, but not more frequently than monthly, by a trade association that receives renter data and publishes it in an aggregated and anonymous matter; or (ii) a product used for the purpose of establishing rent or income limits in accordance with the affordable housing program guidelines of a local government, the commonwealth, the federal government or other political subdivision.
“Coordinating function”, any action utilizing nonpublic competitor data that includes: (i) collecting historical or contemporaneous actual rent prices, supply levels or lease or rental contract termination and renewal dates of residential dwelling units from two or more rental property lessors or landlords; (ii) analyzing or processing of historical or contemporaneous actual rent prices, supply levels or lease or rental contract termination and renewal dates of residential dwelling units from two or more rental property lessors or landlords through use of a system, software or process that uses computation, including by using the information to train an algorithm; and (iii) recommending rental prices, lease renewal terms or ideal occupancy levels to a rental property lessor or landlord.
"Coordinator", any person who operates an algorithmic device, software or data analytics service that performs a coordinating function for any residential rental property lessor or landlord, including a residential rental property lessor or landlord performing a coordinating function for their own benefit.
"Nonpublic competitor data", information that is not widely available or easily accessible to the public, including information about actual rent prices, occupancy rates, lease start and end dates, and similar data, regardless of whether the data are attributable to a specific competitor or anonymized, and that is derived from or otherwise provided by any other lessor or landlord.
“Person”, any natural person or persons, or any corporation, partnership, company, trust or association of persons.
"Residential Dwelling Unit", any house, apartment, accessory unit or other unit intended to be used as a primary residence in the state.
(b) In setting the amount of rent to be charged to a tenant for the occupancy of a residential dwelling unit, determining any change in the amount of rent to be charged to a tenant for the renewed occupancy of a residential dwelling unit, or otherwise determining what amount to charge a tenant to rent a residential dwelling unit, or determining occupancy levels of residential dwelling units, no lessor or landlord shall employ, use or rely upon an algorithmic device or coordinator.
(c) A violation of this section shall constitute a violation of section 2 of Chapter 93A. The civil penalty for each violation of this section shall not exceed $5,000 per violation. For the purposes of this section, each time a rent is determined, increased or otherwise set under subsection (b) shall constitute a single and separate violation.
(d) In the case of any successful action to enforce liability pursuant to this chapter, the costs of the action together with reasonable attorney fees, expert fees and the costs of investigation as determined by the court shall be awarded to plaintiffs. Costs and attorney fees, expert fees and the costs of investigation shall be awarded to the attorney general or municipality where the attorney general or municipality successfully enforces this chapter.

rules.title: Prohibition on obtaining defined coordinator services
rules.requirement: A rental property owner, or its agent, representative, or subcontractor, may not receive, subscribe to, contract for, or otherwise exchange consideration for the use of a defined coordinator’s services. This conduct is unlawful and violates the New Jersey Antitrust Act.
rules.exemptions: A coordinator is a person operating algorithmic revenue management software or an algorithmic device that performs a coordinating function for a rental property owner, including an owner acting for its own benefit. An algorithmic device excludes a spreadsheet operating without artificial intelligence and requiring human analysis to process or calculate data, and a database whose only algorithmic use is querying stored unprocessed data. A coordinating function encompasses collecting two or more owners’ competitively sensitive information for algorithmic or automated analysis used to set or recommend rents, material lease terms, or occupancy levels; setting those terms through an algorithm or automated process analyzing another owner’s competitively sensitive information; or setting or recommending those terms for two or more owners through the same or substantially similar algorithm or automated process facilitating parallel pricing coordination. Rent-regulation exemptions include certificates issued after February 1, 1995 and other applicable Costa-Hawkins exemptions; qualifying mobilehome agreements longer than one year, new spaces first offered on or after January 1, 1990, non-primary-residence mobilehomes not leased to another, and other applicable Mobilehome Residency Law exemptions; specified restricted/subsidized affordable housing; dormitories owned and operated by higher-education institutions or K–12 schools; housing issued a certificate within the previous 15 years; continuously owner-occupied two-unit structures from tenancy inception with neither unit an ADU or junior ADU; and separately alienable dwellings whose owner is neither a REIT, corporation nor LLC with a corporate member and whose tenants receive the prescribed notice, included in agreements commenced or renewed after effectiveness. Petitions proceed under section 8-3145 and applicable regulations; no petition proceeds when a decision on the same or substantially the same grounds was made within the previous 180 days. Applicable standards include reasonable notice to the landlord and an opportunity to correct the conditions. The specified July 1, 2023 commencement subject to Council modification, annual exemption-claim provisions and incorporated statutory exemptions require execution review.

Tenant may submit a Petition to the Program Administrator in accordance with the
procedures set forth in this Division on any one (1) or more of the following grounds:

              1)     To request review of a Rent Increase in excess of the maximum
                     allowed Rent Increase;
              2)     To request a reduction in Rent based on decreased Housing
                     Services;
              3)     To request a reduction in Rent based on failure of the Landlord to
                     maintain a habitable premises, including health, safety, fire, or
                     building code violations;
              4)     To contest a Capital Improvement cost as an unauthorized or
                     excessive pass through; or,
              5)     For any other violation of this Article by the Landlord.

              1)     Tenant receiving a notice of Rent Increase shall have thirty (30)

              2)     In instances where notice is not provided as required, the Tenant
                     shall file a Petition for review of Rent within thirty (30) days after
                     Tenant knew of the alleged failure to comply with the requirements
                     of this Article; and,
              3)     For any other violation(s) of this Article by the Landlord, the Tenant
                     shall file a Petition within one hundred and eighty (180) days of the
                     alleged violation(s).

rules.title: Noncompliance bars landlord petitions and upward adjustments
rules.requirement: No landlord petition or upward rent adjustment under Division 3 is authorized if the landlord continues noncompliance after a Board order or has failed to bring the unit into compliance with the implied warranty of habitability.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to a Landlord seeking a petition or upward adjustment under Santa Ana Division 3 for a Rental Unit subject to that Division, where either stated noncompliance condition exists. Landlord includes owners, lessors, sublessors, successors and representatives with authority to bind the landlord. Rent-regulation exemptions encompass post-February 1, 1995 certificates and other Costa-Hawkins exemptions; qualifying mobilehome leases longer than one year, new spaces first offered on or after January 1, 1990, non-primary-residence mobilehomes not leased to others, and other Mobilehome Residency Law exemptions; specified restricted/subsidized affordable housing; school-owned-and-operated dormitories; certificates issued within the previous 15 years; qualifying continuously owner-occupied two-unit structures from tenancy inception without ADUs or junior ADUs; and separately alienable housing with an owner that is neither a REIT, corporation nor LLC with a corporate member and the prescribed tenant notice, in the agreement for post-effective-date commencements or renewals. Annual exemption claims and incorporated statutory exemptions require execution review.

rules.title: Compliance and registration prerequisites for increases
rules.requirement: A rent increase is ineffective if the owner fails substantial Division 3 compliance, applicable maintenance requirements, or City- or court-ordered repairs. No increase takes effect without accurately completed unit registration.

rules.title: Rental Registry Fee pass-through limit
rules.requirement: After timely payment, a landlord may pass through at most 50% of the Registry Fee in twelve equal monthly installments, excluding it from rent-increase calculations; delinquent fees and penalties cannot be passed through. No portion may be charged to the specified affordable or subsidized tenants, and excess pass-through payments must be reimbursed.

rules.title: Registration prerequisite to advertising and collecting rent
rules.requirement: A landlord may not advertise a covered unit for rent or demand or accept its rent without complete and accurate registration. Petitions, applications, claims, requests and rent increases cannot take effect without accurately completed registration.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to a Landlord with a Santa Ana Rental Unit subject to Article XIX and its Rental Registry requirements, including owners, lessors, sublessors, successors and representatives authorized to bind the landlord. Complete registration requires all City fees and penalties to be paid and a complete, accurate form containing the information required by Division 4 and implementing policies. Registration duties include initial and annual registration, changes of ownership or management, re-registration after vacancy and re-rental, and registration after loss of exemption; annual exemption declarations and supporting documents are required under section 8-3160(d). Rent and termination exemptions are provision-specific, so neither alone establishes exemption from the entire Article or Registry. The stated October 1, 2023 enforcement commencement and the Article's later voter-approval effectiveness require review.

rules.title: Just cause after thirty days of lawful occupancy
rules.requirement: After a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied covered residential real property for 30 days, the owner may terminate only for just cause stated in a written termination notice.
rules.key_value: 30 days of continuous lawful occupancy
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to an Owner offering Santa Ana residential real property for rent, including lessors, sublessors, successors and representatives authorized to bind the landlord, after the tenant's continuous lawful occupancy for 30 days. Termination provisions exclude mobilehomes and mobilehome spaces subject to Civil Code section 798.56. Section 8-3120(e) excludes transient/tourist hotel occupancy; accommodations in nonprofit hospitals, religious facilities, extended-care facilities, licensed elderly residential-care facilities or specified adult residential facilities; dormitories owned and operated by higher-education institutions or K–12 schools; shared kitchen/bath housing where the owner maintains a principal residence; owner-occupied single-family residences, including those renting no more than two units or bedrooms, including ADUs or junior ADUs; duplexes continuously occupied by the owner as a principal residence since tenancy inception; housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the preceding 15 years; and specified deed-restricted or government-agreement affordable/subsidized housing for very-low-, low- or moderate-income households. Separately alienable dwellings are exempt only when the owner is neither a REIT, corporation nor LLC with a corporate member and tenants receive the prescribed notice, included in the rental agreement for tenancies commenced or renewed after ordinance effectiveness, with agreement placement optional for earlier tenancies. Just cause is governed by the specified at-fault and no-fault grounds and their qualifications in section 8-3120(b). Annual exemption-claim requirements and incorporated statutory definitions require execution review.

rules.title: Formal application before criminal-history inquiry

rules.quoted_span:
Prior to conducting any criminal history inquiry regarding an applicant, the landlord or real estate broker shall provide standard written notification to the applicant.

1.

Advising that, upon the written consent of the applicant, the landlord or real estate broker will conduct a criminal history inquiry;

2.
Advising that upon consenting to a criminal history inquiry, the applicant has the right and opportunity of not less than three business days from the receipt of notice to submit evidence which may inform the consideration under Section 2:31-4 of this Article; and

3.

Advising that the applicant has the right to receive a copy, upon the applicant's request, of the results of any criminal history inquiry obtained regarding the applicant.

4.
Attaching a copy of the Information Form Regarding Criminal Record Review - Housing, attached hereto as Appendix A.

c.

A landlord or real estate broker may hold a housing unit open until an applicant provides information about rehabilitation, but a landlord or real estate broker is not required to hold a housing unit after making an initial determination of an applicant's eligibility.

rules.title: Criminal records excluded from inquiry and adverse action
rules.requirement: A landlord or broker must not inquire into, require disclosure of, or take adverse action based on arrests or accusations that are neither pending nor resulted in conviction; erased, expunged, pardoned or otherwise legally nullified records; juvenile delinquency adjudications; or sealed records.

Any arrest or criminal accusation made against such person which is not then pending against that person and which did not result in a conviction;

2.

Any records which have been erased, expunged, the subject of an executive pardon, or otherwise legally nullified; or
3.

Any juvenile adjudications of delinquency or any records which have been sealed.

A landlord or real estate broker shall consider the following factors in evaluating the applicant and the results of any criminal history inquiry, conducted in accordance with the limitations of Section 2:31-3 .

Any information, if provided, pertaining to the degree of rehabilitation and good conduct or to the accuracy of the criminal record in question produced by the applicant, or produced on his or her behalf to the landlord or real estate broker, including but not limited to any certificate of rehabilitation issued by any state or federal agency, which includes but is not limited to certificates issued pursuant to N.J.S.A. 2A:168A-1 to 16;

The amount of time that has passed since the conviction(s) and/or release from custody; and

The nature of and circumstances surrounding the crime(s).

rules.quoted_span:
The Fair Housing Ordinance prohibits discrimination in real estate transactions such as:
viewing or renting an apartment
terms and conditions of tenancy
refusing to reasonably accommodate a person with a  disability if the accommodation would not cause an undue hardship to the landlord
viewing or purchasing a home
applying for or obtaining a mortgage
purchasing homeowners' or renters' insurance
printing, publicizing or advertising housing in a discriminatory manner

(2) A landlord or their agent may charge an applicant an application screening fee only if the landlord or their agent, at the time the application screening fee is collected, offers any of the following:

charged an application screening fee unless or until their application is actually considered.

The landlord may offer, as an alternative to refunding the screening fee, the option, at the applicant’s discretion, for the screening fee paid by the applicant to be applied to an application for another rental unit offered by the landlord. A landlord or their agent shall not be required to refund an application screening fee to an applicant whose application is denied, after consideration, because the applicant does not meet the landlord’s established screening criteria.
(B) An application screening process in which the landlord or their agent returns the entire screening fee to any applicant who is not selected for tenancy, regardless of the reason, within 7 days of selecting an applicant for tenancy or 30 days of when the application was submitted, whichever occurs first.

not perform a personal reference check or does not obtain a consumer credit report, the landlord or their agent shall return any amount of the screening fee that is not used for the purposes authorized by this section to the applicant.

this section, “application screening fee” means any nonrefundable payment of money charged by a landlord or their agent to an applicant, the purpose of which is to purchase a consumer credit report and to validate, review, or otherwise process an application for the rent or lease of residential rental property.

rules.title: Just cause required to terminate a covered tenancy
rules.requirement: A landlord may terminate a covered tenancy only for a specified at-fault cause or a specified no-fault cause pursued in good faith. Each ground remains subject to its statutory qualifications and the applicable notice, cure, relocation, and other termination requirements.
rules.coverage_conditions: Covers dwellings or units intended for human habitation, including units in mobilehome parks, where a natural-person tenant has a lawful right to continuous use or occupancy for more than 30 days; a fixed-term lease of three months or less, including extensions or renewals of three months or less, is excluded. Apply every section 98.0703 exemption: transient/tourist hotel occupancy under Civil Code section 1940(b); short-term residential occupancy defined by and subject to Code Chapter 5, Article 10, Division 1; housing restricted by deed, government agreement, or other document as affordable to very-low-, low-, or moderate-income households; qualifying subsidized affordable housing, except Section 8 tenant-based assistance; mobilehomes subject to the Mobilehome Residency Law; accommodations in a nonprofit hospital, religious facility, extended-care facility, licensed residential care facility for the elderly, adult residential facility, or nonprofit transitional housing; dormitories owned and operated by a higher-education or K–12 institution; a tenant sharing a bathroom or kitchen with a landlord whose principal residence is the property; a landlord-principal-residence single-family residence, including the stated no-more-than-two-bedroom, two-ADU, or two-JADU circumstances and a mobilehome; two separate dwelling units in one structure where the landlord occupies one as a principal residence at tenancy commencement and continuously thereafter; housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the preceding 15 years unless it is a mobilehome; and separately alienable property, including a mobilehome, only when the landlord is neither a REIT, corporation, LLC with a corporate member, nor mobilehome-park management, and tenants receive the prescribed written exemption notice. That notice must be in the lease for tenancies commenced or renewed on or after January 1, 2024; it may be in the lease for earlier tenancies. Nonprofit transitional housing means nonprofit-operated temporary housing for up to 24 months with supportive services directed toward permanent housing. Exact institutional definitions, ownership circumstances, principal-residence timing, and notice requirements require execution review.
rules.exemptions: The landlord definition includes an owner, a person acting as principal or through an agent with the right to offer the property for rent, and a predecessor in interest. At-fault grounds are rent default; material lease breach as described in Code of Civil Procedure section 1161(3), including violation after written corrective notice; statutory nuisance or waste; refusal after written request to renew a written lease that terminated on or after June 24, 2023 for a substantially similar duration and provisions that comply with law; tenant criminal activity on the property or its common areas; a Penal Code section 422(a) criminal threat against the landlord or another tenant regardless of location; prohibited assignment or subletting; refusal of legally authorized entry; unlawful use; failure by a former employee, agent, or licensee to vacate after termination of that status; or failure to surrender possession following the specified written tenant notice or an offer accepted by the landlord in writing. No-fault grounds require honest intent without ulterior motives and are qualified owner/family occupancy, withdrawal from the rental market, specified government/court orders or a local ordinance requiring vacancy, or qualified demolition/substantial remodeling. A habitability order requiring vacancy for fewer than 30 days is not just cause. Owner occupancy and remodeling are subject to the detailed restrictions in section 98.0704(b)(1) and (4).

rules.requirement: An owner invoking owner or family occupancy must satisfy the ownership, lease, vacancy, notice, proof, and good-faith conditions, with the intended occupant moving in within 90 days after the tenant vacates and residing there as a primary residence for at least 12 continuous months. §98.0709 Remedies 
(a) A tenant claiming a violation of this Division may file an action against a 
landlord in a court of competent jurisdiction. 
 
(b) A tenant may seek injunctive relief, equitable relief, and money damages, 
including punitive damages, in a civil action against a landlord for a violation 
of this Division.  
Ch. Art. Div.  
9 8 7 19 
 
San Diego Municipal Code Chapter 9:  Building, Housing and Sign Regulations   
(3-2024) 
 
 
 
(c) A tenant may raise, as an affirmative defense, any violation or noncompliance 
with this Division in any action by a landlord to recover possession of a 
residential rental property. 
 
(d) Any attempt by a landlord to recover possession of a residential rental 
property or any actual recovery of possession of a residential rental property 
in violation of this Division shall render the landlord liable to the tenant in a 
civil action for wrongful eviction for damages of not less than three times the 
actual economic damages. 
 
(e) Any landlord who fails to provide relocation assistance as required by 
section 98.0706(c) shall be liable to the tenant in a civil action for not less 
than three times the required relocation assistance and actual economic 
damages. 
 
(f) In the court's discretion, a landlord who attempts to recover possession of a 
residential rental property in material violation of this Division shall be liable 
to the tenant in a civil action for reasonable attorney’s fees and costs. 
 
(g) The remedies under section 98.0709 are cumulative and may be used in 
addition to any other remedies in this Division or at law, statute, or ordinance. 
 
(h) The City may enforce this Division under Chapter 1, Article 2 of this Code, 
including civil and criminal remedies.

If you own rental property in the City of Los Angeles, it may be subject to the
Just Cause Ordinance
(JCO).  It prohibits terminations of tenancies without just cause and requires relocation assistance for no-fault evictions.
Rental Units Covered Under JCO
The JCO covers most residential properties in the City of Los Angeles that are not regulated by the City’s Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO).
In order to apply to a tenancy, it requires that the tenant either has lived in the same unit for at least six months or that their original lease expired, whichever comes first.  There are other specific exceptions to the JCO including, but not limited to, transient hotels, licensed care facilities, fraternity or sorority houses, owner’s roommate, cooperatives under certain circumstances, some non-profit facilities for the homeless or short-term treatment centers for substance abuse, and some properties owned by HACLA or the government.  The JCO can apply to buildings that are newer than October 1, 1978.  The JCO can apply to a property that contains only one single-family dwelling.

rules.title: Provide and post the Notice of Renters’ Protections
rules.requirement: All landlords of residential properties must provide a Notice of Renters’ Protections to tenants who begin or renew their tenancy on or after January 27, 2023. Landlords must also post the notice in an accessible common area of the property.

rules.title: Rent arrears must exceed Fair Market Rent for nonpayment eviction
rules.requirement: Landlords of RSO or JCO rental units may not evict a tenant for falling behind in rent unless the amount owed exceeds the Fair Market Rent applicable to the unit’s bedroom size.

rules.coverage_conditions: Rental units in Los Angeles covered by either the City's RSO or JCO. The source does not define RSO eligibility.
